title: Behavioral and Developmental Manifestations

html:
If empowerment is a drive to maximize the reliable causal influence of action on sensation, then its behavioral signature is not "novelty seeking" per se, but a persistent preference for contingency: organisms will choose situations where (i) their actions produce detectable changes and (ii) those changes are lawfully coupled to specific action choices. In classic motivational language, this is the "effectance/competence" motive: an intrinsic pull toward experiences that yield a feeling of efficacy even when no primary deprivation is in play 1.

Newborn behavior is dominated by reflex arcs and low-dimensional control; empowerment is initially near-zero because the actuator →\rightarrow sensor channel is weak, noisy, and poorly calibrated. Across the first months, infants rapidly allocate attention toward and learn from events that are response-contingent, treating contingency itself as valuable (and its violation as salient) 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8. The mobile conjugate reinforcement paradigm provides the canonical demonstration: infants whose ankle is tethered to an overhead mobile dramatically increase their kick rate and display sustained positive affect, while yoked controls receiving identical but non-contingent visual stimulation do not 9, 10. The reinforcing signal is the contingency itself–the mutual information I(A;S′)I(A;S')–not the sensory richness of the mobile’s motion. This interpretation is strengthened by the finding that when a previously learned contingency is extinguished, infants as young as 2 months display anger rather than mere disinterest 11, suggesting that the expected empowerment signal functions as a reference point whose violation elicits aversive arousal–a primitive "empowerment prediction error." A 2025 experiment studies action–outcome contingencies (Figure) 32. Movement profiles are compared across connected and unconnected limbs (Figure).

Developmental milestones (reaching, sitting, crawling, walking, speech articulation) can be read as successive bandwidth expansions of the action channel: each newly controllable degree of freedom increases the size of the reachable future state set H(St+k!∣st)H(S_{t+k}!\mid s_t), while practice/refinement reduces H(St+k!∣st,A)H(S_{t+k}!\mid s_t, A) by making outcomes more deterministic. On this view, "practice" is empowerment optimization: repetition is not mere motor babbling but an intrinsic program to tighten the action→\rightarrowoutcome mapping while broadening the controllable manifold 1, 2. Piaget’s taxonomy of circular reactions tracks an orderly expansion of where empowerment is sought (and at what level of abstraction) across the first 18 months 12: A developmental experiment tests how reaching adapts to changed visual feedback (Figure) 34. The study compares reaching adaptation across ages (Figure).

Primary circular reactions ("motor babbling"; 1-4 months): discover controllable contingencies within the body itself (proprioceptive empowerment)

Secondary circular reactions (4-8 months): extend controllability to distal objects and simple tool-like interactions

Tertiary circular reactions (12-18 months): systematically vary actions to map the causal geometry of the action-outcome channel–effectively probing its local channel capacity via intervention.

There is evidence that social empowerment is present from early infancy: even before robust object control, infants are sensitive to social contingencies and preferentially engage in interactions where their actions (vocalizations, gaze, affect) reliably elicit responses from caregivers. These early turn-taking loops constitute a high-gain social control channel, supporting the idea that empowerment over other agents is not a late add-on but an early, evolutionarily prepared target of intrinsic control-seeking 5, 13. A longitudinal study observes infant vocalizations during play (Figure) 33. The study also examines infant responses to caregivers (Figure).

The ubiquity of play across mammals and birds provides perhaps the most direct behavioral evidence for empowerment as an intrinsic motivation. Play is metabolically costly, carries non-trivial injury risk, and by definition yields no immediate instrumental payoff–yet it is a robust developmental invariant across altricial species 14. The empowerment framework offers a unifying account: each major category of play maps onto a distinct component of the channel-capacity objective. Object play (manipulating, dropping, mouthing, and disassembling novel items) systematically probes the dynamics of the action-outcome mapping, reducing the conditional entropy H(St+k|st,At:t+k)H(S_{t+k}|s_t, A_{t:t+k}) by building forward models of object physics–how things break, bounce, roll, and deform under varied forces. Locomotor play (running, jumping, climbing in varied and exaggerated patterns) expands the effective motor repertoire, increasing the "alphabet size" of the action channel and thereby the achievable diversity of reachable futures H(St+k|st)H(S_{t+k}|s_t). Social play–particularly rough-and-tumble play 15–involves learning to influence non-stationary agents, arguably the highest-dimensional empowerment challenge, as the "channel" now includes another adaptive system whose (partially observable) transition dynamics must be simultaneously modeled and controlled. A preschool experiment examines exploratory choices (Figure) 35. The authors analyze how novelty and learning progress relate to exploration (Figure).

Several features of play are specifically predicted by the empowerment framework but are puzzling under purely curiosity-driven or skill-practice accounts. First, play is preferentially performed under low-risk, "relaxed field" conditions–satiated, in familiar territory, in the proximity of attachment figures 16–precisely the conditions under which the risk term of EFE is slack and the empowerment term would dominate the agent’s objective. Second, play is characteristically repetitive with variation: animals repeat action sequences but introduce small perturbations, consistent with an agent that is not merely sampling novelty (which would favor maximal variation) but is refining its estimate of the local channel capacity [Intrinsically Motivated Learning of Real World

Sensorimotor Skills with Developmental Constraints]–iteratively testing how reliably distinct actions yield distinguishable outcomes. Third, play peaks during the juvenile period 17 when the organism faces the greatest gap between its current motor/social competence and the full affordance structure of its ecological niche–i.e., when the marginal return on empowerment investment is highest. Moreover, play is not randomly directed across the difficulty spectrum but is preferentially targeted at challenges just beyond current mastery–the same "zone of proximal development" discussed for compression progress (see "Intrinsic Motivation" section), but measured in a different currency. Where compression progress peaks at the frontier of learnability, empowerment gain peaks at the frontier of controllability: tasks where the agent has partial but incomplete command of the action-outcome mapping, so that marginal effort yields the largest increase in ℰ\mathcal{E}. Fully mastered contingencies offer zero marginal empowerment; wholly uncontrollable dynamics offer zero as well. Csikszentmihalyi’s flow state 18 may mark the joint optimum where both gradients are steepest–the task is simultaneously learnable-but-not-yet-learned and controllable-but-not-yet-controlled.

The empowerment framework makes strong predictions about what happens when the action-outcome channel degenerates, and these predictions are borne out across species. Learned helplessness 19, 20 provides the paradigmatic case: organisms exposed to inescapable aversive stimulation–where I(A;S′)≈0I(A;S') \approx 0 by experimental design–subsequently fail to learn avoidable escape, exhibit dramatically reduced exploration, and display depression-like symptomatology including anhedonia, passivity, and appetite disruption. In information-theoretic terms, persistent experience of a zero-capacity channel causes the agent to update its generative model such that empowerment is near-zero across the state space, collapsing the motivational gradient that would normally drive action selection. The connection to clinical depression is well established: the reformulated helplessness theory’s emphasis on attributional style–global, stable, internal attributions for uncontrollable events 21–can be read as the agent’s generative model overgeneralizing the zero-empowerment estimate from one context to the entire state space, a catastrophic prior update that renders all actions equally futile. At the trait and cognitive level, empowerment surfaces as stable beliefs about controllability that modulate behavioral engagement. Bandura’s self-efficacy construct–the belief that one can execute the actions required to produce desired outcomes 22–predicts whether coping behavior is initiated, how much effort is expended, and how long the agent persists under difficulty; in channel-capacity terms, self-efficacy is a meta-estimate of one’s own empowerment, and low self-efficacy functions analogously to a low estimated ℰ\mathcal{E} that preemptively suppresses policy search. Rotter’s locus of control 23 captures a similar dimension: whether the agent models outcomes as contingent on its own actions (internal locus, high estimated I(A;S′)I(A;S')) versus determined by luck, chance, or powerful others (external locus, low estimated I(A;S′)I(A;S')). Langer’s (1975) illusion of control findings–where subjects behave as if they exert causal influence over demonstrably chance events 24–suggest the empowerment computation is systematically biased toward overestimation, consistent with an asymmetric loss function in which underestimating controllability (risking learned helplessness) is more fitness-costly than overestimating it; the bias is strongest when situational cues resemble skill contexts (choice, competition, familiarity), indicating that the system defaults to an agency-assuming prior that must be actively overridden by strong evidence of uncontrollability. Self-determination theory identifies competence (perceived effectance over the environment) and autonomy (perceived self-causation of behavior) as two of three basic psychological needs whose satisfaction is necessary for wellbeing and whose frustration reliably impairs intrinsic motivation 25, 26. The overjustification effect–the well-replicated finding that tangible external rewards undermine pre-existing intrinsic motivation 27, 28–is particularly telling: when the perceived locus of causality shifts from internal to external, the agent’s estimate of its own channel capacity decreases (it models itself as a passive conduit for externally specified behaviors rather than an autonomous source of causal influence), and intrinsic motivation collapses accordingly. Collectively, these phenomena suggest that organisms continuously monitor and defend their empowerment, and that sustained deprivation of controllability produces motivational and affective pathology that is not reducible to the absence of reward. A human stress experiment manipulates controllability (Figure) 36. The human imaging study compares controlled and uncontrolled conditions (Figure).

Across taxa, organisms exhibit strategies for amplifying channel capacity beyond the limits of their native actuator-sensor loop, and these strategies scale from concrete sensorimotor extensions to abstract institutional design. Tool use–documented in corvids, primates, cetaceans, and other lineages 29–literally expands the set of physically reachable states: a chimpanzee wielding a stick probe can access food items that are unreachable without it, directly increasing H(St+k|st)H(S_{t+k}|s_t), and the drive to acquire, cache, and iteratively refine tools is consistent with an agent that assigns intrinsic value to states of higher empowerment independent of any single consummatory goal. Territorial behavior can be similarly reframed: maintaining exclusive access to a spatial domain ensures continued access to a diversity of resource patches and microhabitats (preserving high reachable-state entropy) while excluding competitors whose presence would inject stochastic disruption into the action-outcome mapping (increasing H(St+k|st,At:t+k)H(S_{t+k}|s_t, A_{t:t+k}) as a noise source). Similarly, niche construction can be viewed as the externalization of empowerment: by building nests, roads, or writing systems, organisms restructure the physical world to lower the conditional entropy of future interactions (H(S|A)H(S|A)). A paved road, unlike a chaotic forest floor, ensures that a specific motor command (astepa_{step}) results in a highly predictable displacement (slocs_{loc}), thereby increasing the reliability of the agent-environment channel.

In humans, the empowerment drive appears to generalize far beyond sensorimotor contingencies. The robust preference for choice–demonstrated even in non-human animals such as pigeons 30 and monkeys and rats 31–persists even when additional options do not improve expected outcomes, reflecting valuation of the state-space entropy term itself rather than any particular reachable state. Langer’s (1975) illusion of control findings–where subjects behave as if they exert causal influence over demonstrably chance events 24–suggest the empowerment computation is systematically biased toward overestimation, consistent with an asymmetric loss function in which underestimating controllability (risking learned helplessness) is more fitness-costly than overestimating it. At the largest scale, distinctly human capacities for cumulative culture and institutional design can be read as mechanisms for abstract empowerment preservation: the accumulation of resources and skills beyond immediate need, the invention of property rights that formalize exclusive state-access, financial instruments that convert current assets into diversified future options, and political freedoms that protect the individual’s channel capacity against coercive reduction–all suggest that empowerment maximization, once liberated from concrete sensorimotor channels by model-based cognition, becomes a dominant organizing principle of human behavioral ecology.
